blocks.text: Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland synthesises and secretes excessive quantities of thyroid hormones (thyroxine T4 and triiodothyronine T3).
Thyrotoxicosis refers to the clinical and biochemical state resulting from excessive circulating thyroid hormones, regardless of their source.

items.text: Hyperthyroidism: Excessive production and secretion of thyroid hormones by the thyroid gland.
Thyrotoxicosis: Excess thyroid hormone action from any cause, including thyroiditis and excessive exogenous thyroid hormone administration.

blocks.text: **A. Primary hyperthyroidism**

**B. Secondary hyperthyroidism**
Results from excessive stimulation of the thyroid gland by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

**Graves' disease**
An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate TSH receptors, resulting in excessive thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion.
It is the commonest cause of hyperthyroidism in many populations.

blocks.text: Medical emergency – ICU management
Thyroid storm requires simultaneous supportive care and treatment directed at four principal mechanisms:

items.text: Block release of stored thyroid hormones.

blocks.text: **A. Propylthiouracil (PTU)**
Step 1 – Antithyroid treatment
**Prescription 9: PTU in thyroid storm**

items.text: Route: Oral, nasogastric tube or rectal where an appropriate preparation is available.
Duration: Until clinical stabilisation, followed by dose reduction and specialist review.

blocks.text: **Administration:** Give the loading dose first. Ensure adequate delivery, particularly in patients who are vomiting or unable to swallow.
PTU is traditionally preferred in thyroid storm because it inhibits both thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.
However, current evidence has not established a clear mortality advantage over methimazole.
**Alternative: Methimazole/carbimazole**
**Prescription 10: Methimazole in thyroid storm**

items.text: Duration: Until clinical stabilisation, followed by dose reduction.

blocks.text: Carbimazole 80–100 mg/day is an approximate alternative where methimazole is unavailable.
Methimazole or carbimazole may be preferred when significant PTU-associated hepatotoxicity is a concern.
**B. Iodine**
Step 2 – Block hormone release
**Prescription 11: Lugol's iodine**

items.text: Dose: 5–8 drops, depending on the preparation.
Duration: Usually a short course, commonly up to 7–10 days, with specialist review.

blocks.text: **Administration:** Start at least one hour after the first antithyroid drug dose. Dilute in an appropriate liquid before administration.
An alternative is SSKI, commonly 5 drops every 6 hours, but its iodine concentration must be verified.
Iodine is not routinely useful in destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyrotoxicosis.
**C. Hydrocortisone**

**Prescription 12: Hydrocortisone**

items.text: Duration: Until clinical stabilisation, followed by reassessment and discontinuation or tapering as appropriate.

blocks.text: **Administration:** Reconstitute according to the specific vial instructions. Administer by slow IV injection or infusion as appropriate.

**Prescription 13: Propranolol in thyroid storm**
